title: Preface
summary: Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K is its annual report for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2025. It identifies the company, its Delaware incorporation, address, phone, and registered common stock and debt securities on the NYSE; reports no Section 12(g) securities; and provides filing, issuer-status, internal-control, restatement, and shell-company certifications. It states nonaffiliate market value and shares outstanding, and notes that portions of the 2025 proxy statement are incorporated by reference into Parts II and III.

title: Walmart Inc. Form 10-K For the Fiscal Year Ended January 31, 2025
summary: Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2025, lists sections on business and risk factors; cybersecurity, properties, legal proceedings, and mine safety; market and stockholder matters; management’s discussion and analysis; market risk; financial statements; accounting and disclosure controls; other information; governance, executive compensation, ownership, related-party matters, and auditor fees; exhibits and financial statement schedules; a Form 10-K summary; and signatures.

title: ANNUAL REPORT ON FORM 10-K FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JANUARY 31, 2025
summary: Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K covers the fiscal year ended January 31, 2025. References to Walmart Inc. and related terms in the report, incorporated proxy-statement information for the June 5, 2025 annual shareholders’ meeting, and report exhibits generally mean the Delaware corporation and its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise specified or required by context.

title: PART I

nodes.title: Cautionary Statement Regarding Forward-Looking Statements
nodes.summary: The text cautions that Walmart’s forward-looking statements—covering economic conditions, business growth, financial and operating measures, investments, workforce, currency, shareholder returns, liquidity, taxes, regulation, litigation, accounting standards, and social and sustainability goals—are estimates based on assumptions, may differ materially from actual outcomes, and should not be relied on as guarantees; Walmart generally disclaims updating them. It then describes Walmart’s omni-channel retail strategy, customer reach, pricing philosophy, segments, fiscal year and 2025 revenue, headquarters and stock listing; traces its development from 1945 through retail, international and eCommerce expansion; and outlines its stores, digital platforms, membership, services, workforce, global operations, and three reportable segments.

nodes.title: Walmart’s Development and Business Segments
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its global, technology-enabled omnichannel retail strategy, customer reach, everyday-low-price and cost principles, fiscal-year basis, 2025 revenue, headquarters and stock listing. The company’s history spans its founders’ variety stores, discount and supercenter formats, international expansion, eCommerce, acquisitions, pickup and delivery, and continued investment in stores, digital services, associates and offerings such as Walmart+, advertising, marketplaces and financial services. Its operations span multiple regions and comprise Walmart U.S., Walmart International and Sam’s Club U.S., whose sales contributions are generally consistent; further details appear in the financial statements.

nodes.title: Walmart U.S. Segment
nodes.summary: The text describes Walmart’s U.S. and International segments: their scale, locations, formats, brands, fiscal 2023–2025 sales and shares of consolidated sales; omnichannel services, store sizes and Walmart+ benefits; merchandise categories, private and licensed brands, and additional advertising, marketplace, financial and other services; and distribution networks, facilities and shipping methods. It also outlines International’s countries, ownership and portfolio changes, strategy, pickup locations, local brands and supplier relationships, plus regional digital, financial and healthcare offerings.

nodes.title: Sam's Club U.S. Segment
nodes.summary: Sam’s Club U.S. is a membership-only retailer operating 600 clubs across 44 states and Puerto Rico, plus samsclub.com. Fiscal 2025 net sales were $90.2 billion (13% of consolidated sales), versus $86.2 billion in 2024 and $84.3 billion in 2023; membership income significantly contributes to operating income. Club and Plus memberships differ in fees, add-on limits, and benefits; all include a household card, and members can earn redeemable Sam’s Cash. Omni-channel services include curbside pickup, Scan & Go, and Just Go; clubs average about 134,000 square feet. Merchandise spans grocery, general merchandise, health and wellness, and fuel/other, including the expanding Member’s Mark brand; category presentations may be revised for comparability. Distribution uses 31 dedicated facilities, some Walmart facilities, company trucks and carriers, supplier deliveries, and club, fulfillment-center, and distribution-center shipping for online orders.

nodes.title: Other Information
nodes.summary: The company faces intense, evolving competition across physical and online retail and related services, competing on price, assortment, service, convenience, locations, and digital and delivery experiences. Its strategies include everyday low prices and costs, omnichannel pickup and delivery, and expanding digital advertising, marketplace, fulfillment, health, wellness, and financial services. Sales are seasonal, typically peaking in the fiscal fourth quarter. Its global supplier network supports merchandise sourcing and availability; suppliers must meet legal standards. The company protects and licenses intellectual property, and its global operations are subject to varied U.S. and international laws and regulations.

nodes.title: Our Shared Value Priorities
nodes.summary: Walmart seeks long-term shared value by serving stakeholders, building trust and opportunity, managing risks and costs, and strengthening capabilities and systems. It prioritizes issues most relevant to its business and stakeholders where it can act effectively, grouped into four themes: opportunity (jobs, career pathways, belonging, and supplier growth); sustainability (supply-chain resilience and dignity, safer products, nature, waste, renewable energy, and emissions); community (affordable access, quality jobs and training, local suppliers, and community support); and ethics and integrity (compliance, governance, responsible public policy and technology, and human rights). Walmart periodically reports on ESG priorities, strategies, progress, and challenges online, and states that these disclosures are not incorporated into its Form 10-K or other SEC filings.

nodes.title: Human Capital Management
nodes.summary: Walmart’s approximately 2.1 million associates—1.6 million in the U.S.—support its purpose; most U.S. associates are hourly, and 68% are full-time. Its workforce strategy centers on belonging, well-being, growth and digital tools. Belonging efforts include representation reporting, fair-pay and performance practices, and associate feedback channels; the workforce is 51% women globally and 51% people of color in the U.S. Well-being investments include competitive wages, extensive benefits, health services and predictable scheduling, with further information referenced in ESG reporting and financial-statement notes. Growth includes career pathways, training, Walmart Academy and education through Live Better U; about 75% of U.S. salaried store, club and supply-chain managers began in hourly roles. Digital tools aim to improve productivity, engagement and the associate experience.

nodes.title: Our Website and Availability of SEC Reports and Other Information
nodes.summary: Walmart’s corporate website provides free access, as soon as reasonably practicable after SEC submission, to its SEC filings and other shareholder documents; the SEC’s filings website is also identified. SEC filings, senior financial officer reporting protocols, and the Code of Conduct are available online and in print upon shareholder request through Investor Relations. Substantive amendments or waivers of the protocols or the Code for the CEO, CFO, or principal accounting officer will be described under Corporate Governance on Walmart’s website for 12 months.

nodes.title: Information About Our Executive Officers
nodes.summary: The text identifies Walmart’s executive officers as of the 10-K filing, notes that they are elected by and serve at the Board’s pleasure, and says their listed experience generally covers at least five years. It lists each officer’s name, current role and effective date, age, and relevant career history: Daniel J. Bartlett, Rachel Brand, David M. Chojnowski, John Furner, Suresh Kumar, Kathryn McLay, C. Douglas McMillon, Donna Morris, Christopher Nicholas, and John David Rainey.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS

Strategic Risks Failure to successfully execute our omni-channel strategy and the cost of our investments in eCommerce and technology may materially adversely affect our market position, net sales and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company warns that listed risks are not exhaustive and may materially harm its business, results, financial position, and liquidity. Its omni-channel strategy depends on successfully investing in eCommerce, technology (including AI), talent, automation, advertising, acquisitions, partnerships, remodels, and customer initiatives as digital shopping grows. Failure to execute, changing customer perceptions, or reduced store traffic and cross-selling could weaken market position, sales, and performance, and trigger asset impairments. Investment costs and operating losses may hurt near-term results, while failure to realize benefits may harm longer-term performance.

nodes.title: If we do not timely identify or effectively respond to consumer trends or preferences, it could negatively affect our reputation, relationship with our customers, demand for the products and services we sell, our market share and the growth of our business.
nodes.summary: The text warns that failure to anticipate changing consumer demand, preferences, shopping habits, and expectations for price, assortment, experience, convenience, and shipping could reduce sales, market share, growth, and operating results through poor merchandising, inventory, pricing, or promotion decisions. Reputation can be damaged by negative publicity, theft, AI misuse, cyberattacks, or changing societal and political expectations—including scrutiny of DEI and ESG positions—with consequences such as boycotts, investigations, litigation, lost business relationships, and workforce impacts. Inaccurate demand forecasts or ineffective, increasingly complex distribution and fulfillment operations may also cause inventory imbalances, service interruptions, and higher costs; effective network operation is not assured.

nodes.title: We face strong competition from other retailers, wholesale club operators, omni-channel retailers and other businesses which could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company faces intense, rapidly evolving competition across physical, eCommerce, omni-channel, social commerce, wholesale, and related service markets, including from new, well-funded or more agile businesses. Competitors vie for customers, employees, digital visibility, products, and services. Competition centers on price, selection, availability, customer service, locations, convenience, shopping experience, digital platforms and data, and delivery cost, speed, accuracy, and options. Failure to adapt, execute strategy, or keep pace with innovation could materially harm financial performance. Industry consolidation, alliances, bankruptcies, or reduced operations may create stronger competitors with better resources, merchandise access, market reach, and broader offerings at competitive prices, also posing financial risks.

nodes.title: General or macro-economic factors, both domestically and internationally, may materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from macroeconomic conditions, including inflation, interest rates, energy and other costs, unemployment, consumer credit and spending, taxes, regulation, trade barriers, and recessions, which may reduce demand, margins, sales, and inventory turnover, raise expenses, or trigger asset impairments. Strategic alliances and investments may underperform. Pandemics can disrupt demand, staffing, inventory, supply chains, and operations while amplifying other risks. Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical conflict, violence, theft, and transport disruptions may damage or close facilities, limit access and workforce availability, interrupt digital services and product flows, and harm financial results; Hurricanes Helene and Milton affected operations in fiscal 2025 without materially affecting consolidated performance.

nodes.title: Business Alliances and Pandemic Risks
key_items: The performance of strategic alliances and other business relationships to support the expansion of our business could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
Operational Risks Global or regional health pandemics or epidemics could negatively impact our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: Strategic alliances and business relationships, including investments and ventures such as ONE, may underperform expectations, weaken competitiveness, or harm financial results. Global or regional health crises may disrupt operations, demand, inventory, supply chains, costs, workforce access, and financial performance; shift customer behavior and income; and make forecasting difficult. Such crises may also intensify risks involving competition, reputation, strategic initiatives, cybersecurity, payments, technology, labor, litigation, and regulation.

nodes.title: Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical events, catastrophic and other events could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical conflict, violence, theft, and other catastrophic events may disrupt operations and materially harm financial performance. Impacts can include property damage, closures, staffing and access constraints, changing consumer behavior, supply and transport delays, product shortages and higher costs, and interruptions to infrastructure, utilities, banking, or communications. Climate-related physical and transition risks may also raise operating and compliance costs and affect sourcing, communities, and consumer confidence. The company bears losses from damage, inventory loss, and business interruption; U.S.-focused events pose particular risk. Hurricanes Helene and Milton affected fiscal 2025 operations and supply chains but not consolidated financial performance materially.

nodes.title: Risks associated with our suppliers could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company relies on diverse domestic and international suppliers and global sourcing for its financial performance. Risks include difficulty finding compliant, qualified suppliers and obtaining sufficient products on time; supplier financial weakness, capacity or standards failures, labor and raw-material shortages, product safety or quality problems, and pandemic-related or other disruptions. Political and economic instability, extreme weather, transport delays, strikes, costs, security, currency shifts and inflation may also interfere. Trade policies, tariffs, sanctions, barriers and import/export restrictions are outside the company’s control. These factors, including disruptions to logistics and other service providers, could harm operations and financial results.

nodes.title: If the quality or safety of products we sell in stores or online fails to meet our customers' expectations or regulatory standards, we could lose customers, incur liability for any injuries caused by a product we sell or otherwise experience a material impact to our brand, reputation and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from poor-quality or unsafe products sold directly or through third-party marketplaces, including customer loss, injury claims, regulatory enforcement, reputational damage, and financial harm. Supplier indemnities may be inadequate; marketplace legal responsibility is unsettled, seller controls may fail, and counterfeit, infringing, stolen, or prohibited goods create further exposure. It also describes dependence on information systems vulnerable to cyberattacks, outages, disasters, and errors, with recovery, upgrade, and security costs, and warns that failures in online and omnichannel shopping and fulfillment technology could impair results and growth.

nodes.title: Marketplace Product and Information System Risks
key_items: If the quality or safety of products offered for sale on our third-party marketplace fails to meet our customers' expectations or regulatory standards, we could be held directly liable, lose customers, become subject to regulatory enforcement or otherwise experience reputational harm.

We rely extensively on information and financial systems to process transactions, summarize results and manage our business. Disruptions in our systems could harm our ability to conduct our operations.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from unsafe or poor-quality products sold directly or through third-party marketplaces, including customer harm, liability, regulatory action, reputational damage, lost sales, and limits on seller indemnification and compliance controls. It also outlines reliance on information systems and potential outages, cyberattacks, disasters, data loss, and costly repairs, plus disruption and missed benefits from technology updates or integration failures.

nodes.title: If the technology-based systems that give our customers the ability to shop with us online and enable us to deliver products and services do not function effectively, our operating results, as well as our ability to grow our omni-channel business globally, could be materially adversely affected.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks to Walmart’s global omnichannel growth and results if digital platforms, technology, supply chains, or third-party services fail to meet evolving customer expectations. It covers investments in online shopping, pickup and delivery, automation, and AI, alongside AI-related operational, legal, privacy, and regulatory risks. Extensive cybersecurity and privacy threats—including attacks, vulnerabilities, third-party and insider failures, detection and response limits, and breaches involving customer, payment, health, employee, vendor, and VIZIO viewing data—could disrupt sales and operations, harm reputation and competitiveness, and cause litigation, regulatory penalties, remediation costs, and financial losses. It also notes payment-card standards and liabilities, privacy-law notification and compliance obligations, and the inability of controls or insurance to eliminate or fully cover these risks.

nodes.title: Changes in third-party reimbursements and contracts, type or scope of offerings of our health and wellness business could adversely affect our overall results of operations, cash flows and liquidity.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks that pharmacy reimbursement, payer contracts, drug costs and supply, competition, regulation, and health-service offerings may reduce sales, margins, cash flow, or liquidity. It warns that difficulty recruiting and retaining qualified workers, rising labor costs, leadership transitions, and labor-law changes could harm service and performance. Misconduct, fraud, or harm caused by contractors or service providers could damage reputation and increase liability. Financial risks include stock-price declines if results miss market expectations and adverse effects from foreign-exchange fluctuations on reported results.

nodes.title: Operational, Labor, Contractor, and Financial Risks
key_items: Our failure to attract and retain qualified associates, increases in wage and benefit costs, changes in laws and other labor issues could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
Illegal or inappropriate activity of our independent contractors or third-party service providers could expose us to liability and adversely affect our business, reputation and financial performance.
Financial Risks Failure to meet market expectations for our financial performance could adversely affect the market price and volatility of our stock.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks to sales, margins, services, cash flow, and liquidity from pharmaceutical disruptions. Labor shortages, rising wages and benefits, competition for talent, leadership transitions, and changes in employment or healthcare laws could harm service and financial results. Contractor or service-provider misconduct, fraud, injury, or damage could create reputational, regulatory, litigation, and financial exposure. Missing market expectations for sales, growth, earnings, investments, or other initiatives—and changes in dividends, taxes, analyst views, or peer performance—could lower the stock price and increase volatility.

nodes.title: Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates may materially adversely affect our financial performance and our reported results of operations.
nodes.summary: Unfavorable foreign-exchange movements can materially harm Walmart’s financial performance and reported results. International operations use local currencies, while consolidated statements are in U.S. dollars, requiring translation that has previously caused adverse results and may distort period-to-period performance, including Walmart International and consolidated results. Currency changes can also raise the cost of goods purchased in a different currency; if selling prices cannot or will not be adjusted, gross profit may fall. These effects have occurred and may continue.

nodes.title: Legal, Tax, Regulatory, Compliance, Reputational and Other Risks Our international operations subject us to legislative, judicial, accounting, legal, regulatory, tax, political and economic risks and conditions specific to the countries or regions in which we operate, which could materially adversely affect our business or financial performance.
nodes.summary: Walmart’s international operations, which span numerous regions and generated about 18% of fiscal 2025 consolidated sales, face risks that could harm business, financial performance, and reputation. These include political and economic instability; changing laws, regulation, taxes, trade restrictions, sanctions, competition matters, labor, safety, environmental, consumer and data-protection, and anti-money-laundering requirements; currency devaluations and inflation; geopolitical tensions, conflicting laws, and boycotts; operational complexity, tax consequences, and weaker intellectual-property enforcement. Sudden restrictions can be disruptive and costly. Associates, contractors, or agents may also violate applicable anti-corruption or sanctions laws despite company policies and compliance programs, exposing Walmart to penalties and reputational damage.

nodes.title: Changes in tax and trade laws, regulations and interpretations could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Walmart warns that changes to trade policies, tariffs, restrictions, and regulations could raise sourcing costs and selling prices, harming business and financial performance; its U.S. segments account for about 82% of sales. Tax exposure includes uncertain estimates, differing jurisdictional earnings and rates, deferred-tax changes, new laws and reporting duties, transfer pricing, and evolving interpretations. The Tax Act, OECD Pillar Two’s 15% minimum tax, and other domestic and international reforms may increase compliance costs and affect effective tax rates and results. Tax audits and changing rules could make final liabilities differ materially from recorded estimates, affecting income, net income, and cash flows.

nodes.title: Changes in and/or failure to comply with other laws, regulations and interpretations of such laws and regulations specific to the businesses and jurisdictions in which we operate could materially adversely affect our reputation, market position or our business and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text warns that changing or violated laws, regulations, interpretations, and enforcement practices across the company’s markets could increase costs, disrupt operations, restrict business, damage reputation, and harm financial performance. It covers regulation of U.S. healthcare and pharmacy operations, controlled substances, reimbursement, pricing, privacy, fraud and abuse, and financial services; broad rules on competition, safety, labor, trade, data, and consumer protection; and evolving ESG reporting expectations. Privacy regimes worldwide impose growing obligations, costs, penalties, and consumer rights. Regulatory changes, scrutiny, audits, third-party misconduct, and failure to adapt pose further risks. It also details VIZIO’s ongoing FTC privacy order and potential consequences including fines, lost licenses, government-program exclusion, and terminated relationships.

nodes.title: We are subject to risks related to litigation and other legal proceedings that may materially adversely affect our results of operations, financial position and liquidity.
nodes.summary: The company faces extensive litigation, investigations, audits and regulatory proceedings that may be costly, disruptive and materially harm its business, finances, results or liquidity. Matters include packaging and environmental claims; employment, wage-and-hour, competition and consumer-protection class actions; opioid distribution; driver classification and platform practices, including a stayed CFPB case; Flipkart foreign-investment and competition investigations in India; Walmex competition proceedings and penalties in Mexico; and U.S. money-transfer, fraud-prevention and anti-money-laundering matters. Outcomes and potential losses are often uncertain or unestimable; further details appear in the annual report’s legal-proceedings and financial-statement notes. Bylaws also make Delaware Chancery the exclusive forum for certain shareholder claims, potentially raising costs or restricting forum choice, though federal securities-law jurisdiction is unaffected.

nodes.title: Not satisfying stakeholder expectations with respect to our ESG efforts could adversely affect our reputation or subject us to regulatory or litigation risk.
nodes.summary: The company pursues ESG goals and shared value initiatives, including on climate, waste, packaging and plastics, and reports priorities, progress and challenges online. Stakeholder expectations are evolving and diverse, and goals may not be achieved or deliver intended results due to risks beyond the company’s control. Perceived shortcomings may dissatisfy stakeholders, harm reputation, morale or customer and shareholder support, and prompt regulatory challenges or litigation, including class or mass actions.

The section describes strategic, market, operational, technology, financial, legal, regulatory, and reputational risks that could harm Walmart’s business, results, cash flows, liquidity, or market position. These include executing its omnichannel and technology investments; adapting to consumers and competition; economic, pandemic, climate, disaster, geopolitical, supplier, product-safety, system, cybersecurity, privacy, and payment disruptions; pharmacy, workforce, contractor, currency, and market-expectation risks; and international, tax, trade, compliance, litigation, and ESG challenges. Risks may cause lost sales, higher costs, liability, penalties, asset impairments, or reputational damage.

nodes.title: ITEM 1C. CYBERSECURITY
key_items: Board of Directors' oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats; Management's role in assessing and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats
Board of Directors' oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats
Management's role in assessing and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats
Protecting our technology and information systems; Incident response and recovery planning; Third-party risk management; Training and awareness
Protecting our technology and information systems
nodes.summary: Walmart describes cybersecurity as part of enterprise risk management and its commitment to digital trust, protecting information confidentiality, integrity and availability. The Board delegates cybersecurity oversight to the Audit Committee, which receives management updates and incident escalations. The CISO leads the program, supported by multidisciplinary teams and reporting to the CTO. The program draws on NIST-CSF and includes technology safeguards and monitoring, incident response and recovery, third-party risk management, recurring training, and periodic assessments and testing, with external expertise where appropriate. Walmart reports past threats and incidents but no known material impact or reasonably likely material risk as of the report date; future material incidents remain possible, and further risks are discussed in Item 1A.

nodes.title: ITEM 2. PROPERTIES
nodes.summary: As of January 31, 2025, the document reports retail unit counts and square footage for Walmart U.S., Sam’s Club U.S., Walmart International, and the total company, with international dates adjusted by country. It also details owned and leased retail units and distribution facilities, including returns and dedicated eCommerce centers; some distribution facilities are third-party owned and operated. Walmart owns its Bentonville principal office and owns or leases other offices and store land. Independent contractors construct buildings; store leases may include escalating or sales-based rent and renewal options. Further distribution information is referenced in Item 1.

nodes.title: Legal Proceedings, Environmental Matters, and Mine Safety
key_items: I. SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION; II. ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
nodes.summary: Describes Walmart’s ordinary-course legal proceedings and lists opioid-related litigation, settlements and derivative and securities actions, plus False Claims Act, ASDA equal-value, money-transfer, driver-platform, and Mexico and India antitrust matters. Notes that approximately $3.3 billion in opioid settlement liabilities was fully paid by January 31, 2025, with participation deadlines for eligible groups. Reports an EPA Clean Air Act finding concerning refrigeration leak detection and repair; the investigation is ongoing, and its outcome and potential penalties are uncertain. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

nodes.title: ITEM 5. MARKET FOR REGISTRANT'S COMMON EQUITY, RELATED STOCKHOLDER MATTERS AND ISSUER PURCHASES OF EQUITY SECURITIES

Holders of Record of Common Stock
nodes.summary: Walmart’s common stock trades on the NYSE under WMT. As of March 12, 2025, it had 194,162 holders of record, plus a larger number of beneficial owners. A chart compares five-year total shareholder returns through fiscal 2025, assuming a $100 investment and reinvested dividends, against the S&P 500 and its Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retailing Index. Fiscal 2025 repurchases were under the Board-approved $20 billion program, with no expiration; $12 billion remained authorized at January 31, 2025, and repurchased shares are retired. The text also reports monthly repurchase counts, average prices, and remaining authorization for November 2024–January 2025, totaling 15,907,163 shares.

summary: Part I presents Walmart’s forward-looking-statement cautions and company overview, history, business segments, products, services, operations, competition, suppliers, seasonality, intellectual property, and regulatory environment. It covers shared-value priorities and workforce management; access to SEC filings, executive officers, cybersecurity governance, and risk factors; unresolved staff comments; properties and facilities; legal, environmental, and mine-safety matters; and common-stock trading, shareholder returns, and fiscal 2025 share repurchases.

title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

nodes.title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: Management’s discussion covers fiscal 2023–2025 results, financial-statement changes, performance measures, and the results of three business segments. It explains segment operating income, comparable-sales definitions and exclusions, currency-impact calculations, and their limitations. It outlines automation, supply-chain, and earnings-diversification strategies; VIZIO’s acquisition and international portfolio changes. It describes intense retail and talent competition, factors affecting results, pricing and merchandising responses to costs, and expected uncertainty from inflation, tariffs, currencies, economic conditions, employment, and supply chains, with further segment analysis referenced.

nodes.title: Company Performance Metrics
nodes.summary: The company’s priorities are growth through omnichannel service, improved operating margins through productivity and business mix, and stronger investment returns through margin improvement and disciplined spending. Growth initiatives include comparable sales, Sam’s Club U.S. membership, Walmart+, eCommerce, and complementary omnichannel services. Comparable sales measure existing stores and clubs, including eCommerce; the company reports retail-calendar figures in earnings releases but discusses fiscal-calendar figures, and reports U.S. results as a meaningful market measure. U.S. comparable sales rose 4.8% in fiscal 2025 versus 4.9% in 2024. Walmart U.S. rose 4.8% and 5.5%, driven in 2025 by transactions and unit volumes and in 2024 by transactions and average ticket; grocery and health and wellness were strong in both years. eCommerce contributed about 2.9% and 2.6%, mainly through store-fulfilled pickup and delivery. Sam’s Club U.S. rose 4.7% and 2.3%, with 2025 growth from transactions and unit volumes and 2024 growth from transactions and average ticket. The text also presents a table of fuel impacts on comparable sales.

nodes.title: Growth
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to operating results, including economic conditions, costs, tariffs, cybersecurity, unemployment and supply-chain uncertainty, and explains pricing and merchandising responses that may affect gross margin. It states priorities of growth, margin improvement and investment returns, with growth focused on omnichannel shopping, membership and eCommerce. It defines comparable sales and calendar conventions, then reports U.S. results: total comparable sales rose 4.8% in fiscal 2025 and 4.9% in 2024; Walmart U.S. rose 4.8% and 5.5%, and Sam’s Club U.S. 4.7% and 2.3%. Growth drivers included transactions, units, grocery and health and wellness; eCommerce contributions were also reported, while lower fuel sales partly offset Sam’s Club growth.

nodes.title: Margin
nodes.summary: The company prioritizes margin growth through productivity, technology and process improvements, cost and inventory management, expense discipline, and a shift toward higher-margin businesses such as digital advertising and marketplace. It defines expense leverage as sales growing faster than operating expenses and seeks operating income leverage, with operating income growing faster than sales. Fiscal 2025 net sales were $674.5 billion, up 5.0%, versus $642.6 billion in 2024; gross profit rates were 24.1% and 23.7%, operating expense rates 20.7% and 20.4%, and operating income $29.3 billion (4.4% of sales) and $27.0 billion (4.2%). Gross profit rates rose 40 and 27 basis points, driven by Walmart U.S. pricing and growth in higher-margin businesses, partly offset by lower-margin merchandise mix; 2024 also benefited from lapping markdowns. Operating expense rates rose 36 basis points in 2025 due to variable pay, marketing, and depreciation, but fell 60 basis points in 2024 after lapping opioid settlement and international restructuring charges. Operating income rates increased 15 and 83 basis points, respectively, reflecting these factors and strong global membership income growth.

nodes.title: Returns
key_items: Return on Assets and Return on Investment
nodes.summary: Walmart expects returns on capital to improve through its financial framework, tracking return on investment (ROI) and free cash flow and returning capital through share repurchases and dividends. The text defines GAAP return on assets (ROA) and non-GAAP ROI, explains their formulas, limitations, and use in assessing asset deployment, and reconciles ROI to ROA. Fiscal 2025 ROA rose to 7.9% from 6.6% in 2024, mainly due to higher net income; ROI increased to 15.5% from 15.0%, as operating income growth outweighed higher invested capital from property and equipment purchases. Supporting calculations and balance-sheet data for 2023–2025 are provided.

nodes.title: Strategic Capital Allocation
nodes.summary: Walmart prioritizes capital spending on higher-return automation-focused areas, including eCommerce, supply chain, technology, customer initiatives, store and club remodels, and new locations; the table reports fiscal 2024–2025 spending by category and U.S./international totals. The text defines free cash flow (FCF) as operating cash flow less property and equipment payments, explains its supplemental, non-GAAP nature and limitations, and reports operating cash flow and FCF for fiscal 2023–2025. It explains year-over-year changes, reconciles FCF to operating cash flow, and reports investing and financing cash flows, noting investing cash flow includes capital expenditures.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Reports Walmart’s fiscal 2025 and 2024 consolidated and segment results, including sales, comparable sales, membership income, gross profit, operating expenses, operating income, net income, EPS, tax rates, store counts and retail space. Consolidated revenue growth reflected positive comparable sales, transaction and volume growth, eCommerce and grocery/health sales, and higher membership income; currency movements also affected sales. Gross margins improved, while expense-rate changes reflected variable pay, marketing, depreciation, prior-year charges and investments. Net income and EPS rose; investment valuation changes drove non-operating losses and affected taxes, whose rates also reflect Flipkart/PhonePe separation and other factors. Walmart U.S. growth came from comparable sales, eCommerce and membership, with margin gains partly offset by mix and higher expenses. International sales rose despite currency headwinds, with margin and expense leverage improving operating income. Sam’s Club U.S. results cover fuel-inclusive and fuel-excluded measures: sales, membership and margins grew, while fuel prices, product mix, fulfillment costs, compensation and technology spending affected results; excluding-fuel data is provided to clarify fuel-price volatility.

Dividends; Company Share Repurchase Program; Material Cash Requirements
nodes.summary: The text reviews liquidity, cash flows, funding, and capital commitments. Operating cash flow rose to $36.4 billion in fiscal 2025, while cash was $9.0 billion and the working capital deficit widened to $17.1 billion; the company expects liquidity to remain adequate and discusses restricted foreign cash and repatriation. Investing outflows were $21.4 billion, mainly capital spending, with fiscal 2026 capital expenditures projected at $21–25 billion. Financing outflows were $14.8 billion, including debt, dividends, buybacks, and subsidiary transactions. It details short-term borrowing, credit facilities, letters of credit, long-term debt and interest, dividend increases, share-repurchase authorization and activity, and material operating and contractual cash requirements, including $37.2 billion in purchase obligations.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: The company expects operating cash flow, cash on hand, short-term borrowing, and capital-market access to cover anticipated needs and obligations, including seasonal inventory, capital spending, acquisitions, dividends, and share repurchases. As of January 31, 2025, its commercial-paper ratings were S&P A-1+, Moody’s P-1, and Fitch F1+; long-term debt ratings were AA, Aa2, and AA, respectively. Ratings may change or be withdrawn; performance, economic and retail conditions, finances, debt, capitalization, or strategy may affect them. Downgrades could raise borrowing costs, limit market access, or reduce commercial-paper flexibility and prompt more expensive financing. Ratings are not investment recommendations and apply specifically to each security.

nodes.title: Other Matters
nodes.summary: The report’s Note 10, “Contingencies,” covers opioid-related matters and litigation; Asda equal value claims and related indemnification; money-transfer services litigation, an FTC complaint, and a federal investigation into fraud prevention and anti-money-laundering compliance; Spark driver matters; Walmex’s Mexico antitrust proceeding and constitutional challenge; and Flipkart matters concerning Indian foreign-investment rules and antitrust. Related proceedings are listed under Item 3, Legal Proceedings. These and other reported matters are contingent liabilities that may or may not result in material liability.

nodes.title: Summary of Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: The company prepares U.S. GAAP financial statements using judgments and estimates based on past events and expected outcomes; actual results may differ, and management regularly reviews its accounting policies and disclosures. For contingencies, it accrues probable, reasonably estimable losses, discloses material reasonably possible losses, and reviews matters quarterly; unresolved legal or regulatory cases could materially affect its business and financial results. For uncertain tax positions, it recognizes benefits only when they are more likely than not to withstand tax-authority challenge, reassesses them as circumstances change, and applies a minimum recognition threshold requiring judgment and interpretation of complex tax laws.

summary: Reviews Walmart’s fiscal 2023–2025 strategy, performance, financial condition, and outlook. Defines performance measures and comparable-sales conventions, and discusses growth, margins, returns, capital allocation, segment and consolidated results, and the effects of pricing, product mix, membership, eCommerce, costs, currency, and economic uncertainty. Covers cash flows, liquidity, financing, debt ratings, capital spending, dividends, repurchases, and contractual obligations; identifies significant contingencies and litigation; and explains critical accounting estimates for contingencies and uncertain tax positions.

title: ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
summary: The section discusses market risks from interest rates, currency exchange rates and equity investment valuations, noting sensitivity analyses are hypothetical and hold other assumptions constant. Interest-rate exposure from borrowings and debt is partly hedged through fixed/variable debt management and swaps; swap fair value rose $43 million in fiscal 2025. Variable-rate debt was 20% of total debt, and a 100-basis-point rate change would alter annual interest costs by about $0.1 billion. Currency exposure arises from foreign operations, investments and debt; translation effects caused a $2.2 billion accumulated loss. Currency swaps had $1.4 billion and $1.3 billion liability fair values in 2025 and 2024; hypothetical 10% currency and interest-rate changes would affect swap value by $0.6 billion and $0.1 billion. Immaterial forwards hedge purchase commitments. Equity valuation changes produced a $0.8 billion investment loss; investments were valued at $3.0 billion, with a 10% stock-price change affecting value by about $0.3 billion.

title: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA

nodes.title: Independent Auditor’s Report on Walmart’s Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The auditors give an unqualified opinion that Walmart’s 2025 and 2024 balance sheets and its financial statements for the three years ended January 31, 2025, fairly present its financial position, operating results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP. They also report an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of January 31, 2025. The report explains management’s responsibility, the auditor’s PCAOB registration and independence, and audit procedures designed to provide reasonable assurance against material misstatement from error or fraud.

nodes.title: Critical Audit Matter
nodes.summary: EY identifies legal and regulatory contingencies as a critical audit matter because evaluating loss probability and estimating losses required complex judgment; this designation does not change or constitute a separate audit opinion. Auditors tested related controls, examined board minutes and legal materials, consulted counsel, obtained management representations, and assessed disclosures. EY also opines that Walmart maintained effective internal control over financial reporting at January 31, 2025, describing management’s and auditors’ responsibilities, audit procedures, the control framework and its inherent limitations. EY’s consolidated financial statement opinion was unqualified; it has served as auditor since 1969. Reports are dated March 14, 2025.

nodes.title: Walmart Internal Control Audit Opinion

nodes.summary: The independent auditor concluded that Walmart maintained effective internal control over financial reporting in all material respects as of January 31, 2025, under the 2013 COSO framework. The auditor also noted an unqualified opinion on the related 2025 and 2024 consolidated balance sheets and three-year financial statements. Management is responsible for the controls and its assessment; the PCAOB-registered, independent auditor explains its responsibilities and PCAOB-compliant audit procedures, which provide a reasonable basis for its opinion.

Note 1 describes Walmart’s business and three segments; consolidation practices and reporting periods; GAAP estimates; the 2024 three-for-one stock split; and cash-equivalent criteria, balances, international cash holdings, liquidity arrangements, and restrictions on transferring some foreign cash to the U.S.

nodes.title: Walmart Accounting Policies and Cash
nodes.summary: Walmart operates three reportable segments. Its consolidated statements eliminate intercompany activity, consolidate qualifying variable-interest entities, and use the equity method for significant-influence investments; most non-U.S. operations are reported with a one-month lag. U.S. GAAP estimates affect reported balances and results, which may differ from actual outcomes. A 3-for-1 stock split was retroactively reflected, with par-value reclassification. Cash equivalents include investments maturing within three months and card or electronic transactions settling within seven days. The statements detail related bank receivables, overseas cash balances, liquidity arrangements, and cash restricted from transfer to the U.S.

nodes.title: Receivables, Inventory, Property, and Lease Accounting
nodes.summary: Receivables are reported net of credit-loss reserves, arise from customer, supplier, tax, and real estate transactions, and include customer balances of $4.4 billion in 2025 versus $3.7 billion in 2024. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost or market or net realizable value, using segment-specific retail or weighted-average methods and LIFO or FIFO; LIFO estimates are updated quarterly and reconciled at year-end. Property and equipment are recorded at cost, with improvements capitalized and routine maintenance expensed; the page lists asset balances, useful lives, depreciation policies, and related annual expense. Lease accounting covers lease identification, discounted ROU assets and obligations, term and short-term lease rules, and combined lease/non-lease components and variable costs.

nodes.title: Asset Impairment, Goodwill, and Fair Value
key_items: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangible Assets
nodes.summary: Describes impairment reviews for long-lived assets and the accounting, allocation, and annual or event-driven testing of goodwill and acquired intangible assets. Reports goodwill movements by segment, including the VIZIO acquisition, and intangible asset balances and impairment results. Defines fair value measurement and explains recurring fair-value accounting for equity investments; related net investment losses were $0.8 billion, $3.8 billion, and $1.7 billion in fiscal 2025, 2024, and 2023, respectively.

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.summary: The text explains Walmart’s policies for assessing long-lived-asset impairment; accounting for goodwill and acquired intangible assets, including reporting-unit tests and fiscal 2025–2023 impairment results; goodwill movements by segment and VIZIO-related goodwill; intangible-asset balances; fair-value definitions; equity and trading-debt investment accounting and losses; divestiture indemnification liabilities and maximum exposure; supplier-financing terms, obligations, balance-sheet and cash-flow classification; and actuarial estimation, review, and insurance coverage for self-insurance reserves.

nodes.title: Investments, Indemnities, Supplier Financing and Insurance Reserves
nodes.summary: The page describes accounting for equity investments without readily determinable fair values and trading debt securities, including the $1.2 billion Asda investment and its Level 3 valuation. It reports divestiture-related indemnification liabilities and maximum potential payments. It explains supplier financing arrangements, payment terms, the fiscal 2025 obligations rollforward, balance-sheet classification and cash-flow treatment. It also outlines self-insured risks, actuarial reserve estimation and review, insurance coverage, and where reserves are recorded.

nodes.title: Derivative Hedging and Income Tax Accounting
key_items: Fair Value Hedges; Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary: The Company uses derivatives to manage interest-rate and currency risks, with counterparty credit controls, collateral and netting arrangements, and hedge-accounting or fair-value reporting rules. Fixed-to-variable swaps hedge fixed-rate debt as fair value hedges; cross-currency swaps hedge forecasted foreign-currency debt payments as cash flow hedges, with gains and losses treated accordingly. Income taxes cover deferred taxes and enacted rates, valuation allowances and realization estimates, effective tax rates and discrete events, and liabilities, interest, and penalties for uncertain tax positions.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition and Related Accounting Policies
key_items: Redeemable Noncontrolling Interest; Cost of Sales; Payments from Suppliers
Net Sales; Financial, Advertising and Other Services; Membership and Other Income; Gift Cards
nodes.summary: Explains accounting for redeemable noncontrolling interests, including temporary-equity presentation, periodic adjustments, and a Walmart U.S. put option. Describes cost of sales and supplier payments, generally recorded as cost reductions when inventory is sold, with exceptions for distinct services and specific cost reimbursements. Covers recognition of merchandise, eCommerce, and service revenue; membership fees and other income; and gift-card liabilities, redemption, expiration, and estimated breakage income.

nodes.title: Operating Expenses, Advertising and Currency Translation
key_items: Operating, Selling, General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.summary: Operating, selling, general and administrative expenses cover most operating costs, including labor, depreciation, maintenance, utilities, and much distribution-facility warehousing and occupancy. Because only some distribution costs are included in cost of sales, the company’s gross profit and segment expenses may not be comparable with other retailers’. Advertising, mainly digital, television, and print, is expensed as incurred in operating expenses and totaled $5.1 billion, $4.4 billion, and $4.1 billion in fiscal 2025, 2024, and 2023. International subsidiaries’ assets and liabilities are translated at period-end rates, with adjustments in accumulated other comprehensive loss; income statements use average exchange rates.

Defines internal control over financial reporting, its objectives and limitations, and includes the auditor’s signature and date. Presents Walmart’s 2023–2025 financial statements and accounting policies for its business segments, consolidation, estimates, stock split, cash, receivables, inventory, property, leases, impairments, goodwill, fair value, investments, indemnities, supplier financing, and insurance reserves. Also covers derivatives and hedging, income taxes, noncontrolling interests, cost of sales, revenue, memberships, gift cards, operating expenses, advertising, and foreign-currency translation.

nodes.title: Recent Accounting Pronouncements
nodes.summary: The text summarizes three FASB accounting updates. ASU 2023-07 enhances segment disclosures, including significant expenses; the Company adopted it retrospectively for fiscal 2025 and disclosed specified expenses by segment. ASU 2023-09 expands income tax disclosures, applies from fiscal years after December 15, 2024, and will be adopted prospectively for fiscal 2026; its disclosure impact is under evaluation, with no expected effect on financial condition or results. ASU 2024-03 requires disaggregated expense disclosures, applies from fiscal years after December 15, 2026 (interim periods after December 15, 2027), permits early adoption and prospective or retrospective application, and is under evaluation; it affects disclosures only.

nodes.title: Note 2. Net Income Per Common Share
nodes.summary: The note explains that basic net income per Walmart common share uses weighted-average shares outstanding, while diluted earnings per share also reflects dilutive share-based awards under the treasury stock method; no significant antidilutive awards were excluded in fiscal 2025, 2024, or 2023. A reconciliation reports consolidated net income, noncontrolling-interest adjustments, Walmart-attributable income, basic and diluted weighted-average shares, award dilution, and basic/diluted earnings per share for those years.

It details share-based compensation expense, tax benefits, award categories and the 2015 Stock Incentive Plan; explains restricted-stock and performance-unit vesting, valuation and expense recognition; and presents award activity, vested values, unrecognized costs and remaining expense periods. It also outlines the $20 billion repurchase program, remaining authorization, decision factors, and shares, prices and cash paid for repurchases in fiscal 2023–2025.

nodes.title: Note 4. Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss
nodes.summary: The note presents a fiscal 2023–2025 rollforward of accumulated other comprehensive loss, in millions and net of immaterial taxes, showing currency translation and other, cash flow hedges, and total balances, losses, income, and reclassifications. In fiscal 2023, a Massmart noncontrolling-interest buyout caused cumulative currency translation to be reallocated to the Company. Cash flow hedge reclassifications generally affect interest expense, while translation amounts from foreign-bond settlements and related cross-currency swaps affect operating, selling, general and administrative expenses.

nodes.title: Note 5. Accrued Liabilities
nodes.summary: The note reports accrued liabilities of $29.345 billion at January 31, 2025, versus $28.759 billion in 2024. Categories are accrued wages and benefits ($7.897 billion; $8.590 billion), self-insurance ($4.976 billion; $4.916 billion), accrued non-income taxes ($3.503 billion; $3.459 billion), deferred gift card revenue ($2.755 billion; $2.664 billion), and other liabilities ($10.214 billion; $9.130 billion). Wages and benefits include salaries, vacation, bonuses, and incentives; self-insurance covers workers’ compensation, liability, product, and certain healthcare obligations; non-income taxes include payroll, property, value-added, sales, and other taxes; other liabilities include deferred membership revenue, interest, supply chain, advertising, maintenance, and utilities.

nodes.title: Note 6. Short-term Borrowings and Long-term Debt
nodes.summary: Note 6 details short-term borrowings, committed credit facilities, letters of credit, long-term debt balances, rates, maturities, and repayments. Short-term borrowings rose to $3.1 billion in 2025 from $0.9 billion in 2024; $15 billion of credit lines were undrawn, with stated maturities, SOFR-based pricing, fees, and debt covenants. Long-term debt totaled $33.4 billion in 2025 versus $36.1 billion in 2024, with annual maturities through 2030 and thereafter. The note also lists five fixed-rate unsecured notes issued in 2024, their terms and proceeds, and significant debt repayments in fiscal 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Note 7. Leases
nodes.summary: The note describes the Company’s U.S. and international leases of retail, distribution and fulfillment, warehouse, office, land, and equipment assets. It reports operating, finance, and variable lease costs for fiscal 2023–2025; lease-related cash payments and assets obtained in exchange for lease obligations; weighted-average remaining terms and discount rates for operating and finance leases; and, as of January 31, 2025, annual operating and finance lease obligations by maturity, total undiscounted obligations, imputed interest, and net obligations.

nodes.title: Note 8. Fair Value Measurements
key_items: Derivatives; Nonrecurring Fair Value Measurements; Other Fair Value Disclosures
nodes.summary: Note 8 explains the fair value hierarchy: Level 1 quoted active-market prices, Level 2 other observable inputs, and Level 3 unobservable inputs. Recurring Level 1 and 2 equity investments are reported in other long-term assets, with fair value changes in earnings; their value fell $4.2 billion in fiscal 2025, mainly following the JD.com sale, and $3.4 billion in fiscal 2024, mainly from stock-price changes. The August 2024 JD.com sale yielded $3.6 billion net proceeds and a $0.3 billion realized loss. Derivatives are valued using Level 2 interest-rate and currency curves; notional amounts and fair values are presented for 2025 and 2024, with balances primarily classified in deferred income taxes and other. No material nonrecurring fair value measurements existed at either year-end. Cash, restricted cash, and short-term borrowings are carried at cost, approximating fair value; long-term debt is carried at cost and fair-valued using Level 2 inputs, with carrying and fair values disclosed for both years.

It details deferred tax assets, valuation allowances, liabilities, and balance-sheet classification. The company’s $32.4 billion loss and capital-loss carryforwards, expiration profile, and valuation-allowance assessment are described. nodes.summary: The Company provides U.S. and Puerto Rico 401(k)-type plans, with eligibility to contribute immediately in the U.S. and generally after one year in Puerto Rico. After one year of employment, it matches 100% of contributions up to 6% of eligible earnings; matches vest immediately. Participants may contribute up to 50% of pretax earnings, subject to statutory limits. Non-U.S. associates in international countries participate in defined contribution post-employment plans governed by local laws and tax rules. A table is introduced for contribution expense in fiscal 2025, 2024, and 2023, by U.S. and international plans, and in total; no amounts are shown.

It presents fiscal 2023–2025 segment and consolidated revenues, expenses, operating results, pretax income, assets, depreciation, capital expenditures, and U.S./non-U.S. revenues and long-lived assets; notes no material single-country or customer concentration; and disaggregates segment net sales by merchandise category or market, including eCommerce sales and related presentation changes. title: INSIDER TRADING POLICY

nodes.title: I. General Policy Statement Regarding Insider Trading
key_items: C. Walmart Policy; D. Tipping Information
F. Trading in the Securities of Other Companies; G. Applicability of Policy to Former Associates and Directors
F. Trading in the Securities of Other Companies
G. Applicability of Policy to Former Associates and Directors
nodes.summary: Walmart’s March 2025 policy bars officers, employees, and directors from insider trading and improper disclosure. It defines material and nonpublic information, gives examples, and generally requires one full trading day after public release for market absorption. It explains legal and disciplinary consequences; prohibits affected individuals, household members, dependents, and controlled accounts from trading or tipping based on such information, including securities of other companies learned about through Walmart; and covers retirement and stock-plan transactions. It sets pre-clearance rules for restricted-list personnel trading in publicly traded majority-owned subsidiaries, notes related outside-company ownership restrictions, and addresses former personnel, gifts, and Walmart’s own trading, including permitted Rule 10b5-1 plans.

nodes.title: II. Trading Windows
key_items: A. Associates Subject to Trading Windows
B. When You May and May Not Trade
nodes.summary: The policy imposes trading windows on all Directors and specified Associates: officers, Global Leadership Meeting participants, and those with access to sensitive financial reports. Eligible employees may trade from the day after quarterly earnings release through the next-to-last day of the second month of each fiscal quarter, unless otherwise restricted; trading is generally prohibited outside that window, including transactions through benefit plans. Additional restrictions may apply when someone possesses or may be deemed to possess material nonpublic information, or when the Corporate Secretary’s Office imposes a ban; employees should seek guidance rather than decide for themselves. Rule 10b5-1 trading plans may operate outside windows if adopted during an open window without inside information, comply with SEC requirements, receive advance approval, and are followed in good faith without influence over trades. Plans must set trade terms or delegate them independently; amendments require approval, and generally only one plan may be outstanding, subject to approved exceptions. New plans and amendments, including early termination, require submission at least five business days beforehand and representations of no inside information and good-faith adoption. Sales require cooling-off periods: Directors and Section 16 Officers wait until the later of 90 days after adoption or two business days after the relevant Form 10-Q/10-K filing; other Associates wait 30 days. Plan trades need no further pre-approval. Directors and Section 16 Officers must also report certain other pre-set plans adopted while asserting they lacked inside information.

nodes.title: III. Hedging of, and Other Speculative Transactions in, Walmart Stock
key_items: B. Hedging of Walmart Stock Prohibited; C. Other Restrictions on Trading; D. Consequences of Hedging
B. Hedging of Walmart Stock Prohibited
nodes.summary: Walmart prohibits Associates, including officers, and Directors from directly or indirectly hedging or speculating in Walmart stock, including through designees, because such activity can reduce ownership risk or create conflicts with Walmart and its shareholders. Hedging covers transactions or instruments that mitigate or offset stock-value declines, including prepaid variable forwards, swaps, collars, short sales, futures, and exchange funds; a designee is someone acting under an arrangement that enables hedging on an individual’s behalf. The ban applies to compensation-granted and all other directly or indirectly held Walmart stock. Separate restrictions prohibit speculative stock-linked derivatives and transactions that oppose Walmart’s financial interests, including short-selling. Walmart may impose disciplinary or other action for violations or conduct it considers improper.

nodes.title: IV. Pre-Clearance Requirements for Directors, Section 16 Officers, and Senior Executives
nodes.summary: Section 16 officers, directors, and officers at Executive Vice President level or above must request pre-clearance at least two business days before any Walmart securities transaction, including gifts and Trading Plan changes. The Corporate Secretary’s Senior Vice President may deny requests at sole discretion and consult management or counsel. If denied, do not trade or disclose the restriction. Approval does not permit trading while aware of material non-public information or during a closed window or event-specific restriction, and expires after two business days.

nodes.title: V. Other Trading Restrictions and Required Forms Applicable only to Walmart’s Section 16 Officers and Directors
key_items: A. What You Must Do Before You Trade; B. Frequency of a Purchase and Sale or Sale and Purchase; C. Additional Blackout Periods Related to 401(k) and Other Retirement Plans

nodes.summary: Section 16 officers and directors must pre-clear trades at least two business days in advance; avoid matching purchases and sales within six months because profits may be forfeited, and consult the Corporate Secretary about potentially matchable or exempt transactions. Retirement-plan blackout periods prohibit trading. Officers must timely file required SEC and NYSE forms, report transactions within one business day with specified details, and promptly disclose early termination of trading plans; transaction timing is when commitment becomes irrevocable. Rules extend to household members, dependents, controlled accounts and entities, and beneficially owned securities. Late filings may be disclosed in Walmart’s proxy statement. Margin-loan collateral is prohibited; non-margin pledges require approval two weeks ahead and do not count toward ownership guidelines. The policy also states contact information, Walmart’s right to modify it, and at-will employment terms.

nodes.title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm (intro)
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporating its March 14, 2025 reports on Walmart Inc.’s consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting into 19 specified registration statements (Forms S-3, S-3 ASR, and S-8) covering employee benefit and stock plans, common stock, and debt securities. The reports are included in Walmart’s 2025 Form 10-K for the year ended January 31, 2025. The consent is signed in Rogers, Arkansas, on March 14, 2025.

nodes.title: Exhibit 31.1
nodes.summary: Exhibit 31.1 is Walmart CEO C. Douglas McMillon’s certification of the company’s Form 10-K. He states he reviewed the report, believes it contains no material misstatements or omissions, and that its financial information fairly presents Walmart’s condition and results. He and the other certifying officer are responsible for disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, including their design, evaluation, and reporting material quarterly changes. They also disclosed significant control deficiencies or weaknesses and relevant fraud to the auditors and Audit Committee. Dated March 14, 2025.

nodes.title: Exhibit 31.2
nodes.summary: Exhibit 31.2 is CFO John David Rainey’s March 14, 2025 certification of Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K. He confirms he reviewed the report, believes it contains no material misstatements or omissions, and that its financial information fairly presents Walmart’s condition, results, and cash flows. He describes his and the other certifying officer’s responsibilities for designing, evaluating, and reporting on disclosure controls and internal financial controls, and confirms they disclosed significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and relevant fraud to the auditors and Audit Committee.

nodes.title: Exhibit 32.1
nodes.summary: Exhibit 32.1

summary: Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporating its March 14, 2025 audit reports on Walmart’s consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting into 19 specified registration statements. The section also includes CEO C. Douglas McMillon’s and CFO John David Rainey’s certifications of the 2025 Form 10-K, affirming their review, the report’s accuracy and fair presentation, their responsibilities for disclosure and financial controls, and disclosure of significant control issues and relevant fraud. title: CERTIFICATION PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350 (AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002)
key_items: A. Case Citations For Pending State Court Cases as of March 10, 2025
B. Case Citations For Pending Non-MDL Federal Court Cases as of March 10, 2025
C. Case Citations For Pending Canadian Cases as of March 10, 2025
summary: Walmart CEO C. Douglas McMillon and CFO John David Rainey certify under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 that the company’s January 31, 2025 Form 10-K complies with applicable Exchange Act requirements and fairly presents its financial condition and operating results; both certificates are effective March 14, 2025. Exhibit 99.1 lists pending non-MDL opioid litigation cases as of March 10, 2025, grouped into state-court cases, non-MDL federal cases, and Canadian cases, with parties, courts, and filing dates.
